idiom_name: func(yield func(T) bool) wrapped as iter.Seq[T], driven by for range
implementation_notes: Since Go 1.23 a generator is a function that takes a yield callback (iter.Seq[T] or iter.Seq2[K, V]) and is driven by for range: the producing routine is ordinary code, each yield call emits one element, and the consumer's break becomes yield returning false, so production stops exactly where the loop stops and nothing leaks. It is the language-blessed lazy producer - no goroutine, no channel, no leak on early exit - so prefer it over the channel generator whenever the toolchain allows; the callback may return false for any reason, which is also how filters stop early.
pitfalls: yield's bool result must be honoured: ignoring it keeps producing after the consumer's break and, in an infinite generator, never returns.

The generator body runs on the consumer's goroutine inside the range loop, so a blocking call, a panic or a long step is paid on the consumer's stack - keep per-element work bounded or hand off to the concurrent variant.

Two packages cannot share an iterator type unless they agree on iter.Seq; re-export it (type Seq[T any] = iter.Seq[T]) instead of defining a structurally identical look-alike, which would not be assignable.

variants.name: Goroutine generator feeding a channel (classic)
variants.idiom_name: func() <-chan T with a producer goroutine sending and defer close(out)
variants.implementation_notes: Pike's generator: the function starts a goroutine that produces values and sends each one on a channel, closing it when the sequence ends, while the consumer ranges over the channel. The unbuffered send blocks until the consumer is ready, so a slow consumer throttles production, and it is the only pre-1.23 option - and still the right shape when production must run concurrently (I/O, multiple sources) or on its own goroutine.
pitfalls: A consumer that breaks out of the range leaves the producer blocked on send forever: the goroutine leaks unless the producer selects on a done channel or a context.

An unbuffered channel makes every element a rendezvous (two scheduler switches per item); a buffered channel removes the synchronisation but produces ahead of demand, which hides backpressure problems instead of expressing them.
